extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, political-communication scholars, and journalists interested in news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and testable hypotheses about which characteristics of world events make them likely to be selected, emphasized, and presented as foreign news in newspapers; includes list of factors (F1–F12) and hypotheses about how they combine. Applied to content analysis of newspaper coverage of crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency (F1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'frequency' of an event: the time-span needed for the event to unfold and acquire meaning; events whose temporal frequency fits the publication frequency of the news medium are more likely to be recorded as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/explanation: murders and sudden accidents fit the daily news cycle; long-term developments (e.g., building a dam) will go unreported by a daily unless they reach a dramatic climax (inauguration). The medium's own frequency (daily, weekly, monthly) matters: lower-frequency publications correct for under-reporting of trends. Empirical implication: dailies under-report slow trends; short-span, rapidly unfolding events are advantaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Events must exceed a threshold of salience/importance before being reported at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as a minimum 'signal' that an event must pass (akin to a radio signal passing a loudness threshold). There is a dichotomous idea that an event either passes the threshold and can become news or does not. Threshold interacts with other factors (e.g., a culturally proximate event may need a lower threshold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute intensity / Amplitude (F3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the absolute intensity (size, magnitude, dramatic force) of an event, the more probable it will be recorded as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: larger dams, more violent murders make bigger headlines ceteris paribus. This is analogous to radio 'signal strength' — bigger events are more likely to be noticed. Also conceptualized in dichotomous terms: events above a certain amplitude are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity increase / Dramatic change (F4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that show an increase in intensity (a dramatic change or climax) are more newsworthy than slowly evolving steady phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inaugurations (completion points) draw attention where the long construction process did not. Sudden escalations or acute incidents are favored over slow processes unless they produce a clear climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity / Clarity (F5 / 'signal vs noise')
rubrics_metrics.description: Less ambiguous events — those with a clear, one-dimensional interpretation — are more likely to be noticed and reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An event with a clear interpretation (few, consistent meanings) is preferred to complex, ambiguous events from which many inconsistent implications can be drawn. News selection favors clarity of meaning over complexity; consensual interpretation aids selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness (F6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are meaningful to the audience are more likely to be selected; 'meaningful' includes cultural interpretability and relevance to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two major senses: (a) cultural proximity — events similar to the listener/reader's cultural framework are easier to interpret (ethnocentrism operates); (b) relevance — events in distant places can still be meaningful if they imply consequences for the reader (e.g., conflicts involving one's own group). Example: a North European listener ignores unfamiliar Arab programming but prefers European content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance (F5/F7 in text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events consonant with pre-existing mental images, expectations or wants are more likely to be registered as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonance has both cognitive (predictive) and normative (desire) senses: people more readily receive events that fit their pre-image of reality. This means 'news' often corresponds to 'olds' — items that confirm expectations. However, consonance interacts with unexpectedness (see separate factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness / Rarity (F6/F12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the set of events that are meaningful and consonant, those that are unexpected or rare have the highest chances of being included as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpectedness means both rarity and lack of predictability. Routine, institutionalized, repetitive events attract less attention ceteris paribus. Planners of predictable events (e.g., summit meetings) know this; news tends to favor the ad hoc and surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability / Unpredictability (subfactors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictability (or its converse, unpredictability) of an event affects news selection: predictable events may be less newsworthy; unpredictable events attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability is tied to consonance and unexpectedness. The authors treat predictability as a subdimension that interacts with other factors: unexpectedness (unpredictability) increases newsworthiness, especially when embedded in a meaningful/consonant frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are scarce or rare have higher news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scarcity increases newsworthiness by making information relatively novel; this is closely connected to unexpectedness and rarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity / Persistence (F7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once something has been defined as news and has hit the headlines, it tends to remain news for some time even if the immediate amplitude diminishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: inertia in the system, justification for earlier attention, and the process by which the unexpected becomes familiar. This continuity means items can receive prolonged coverage beyond their initial objective importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition / Balance (F8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial desire to present a 'balanced' news package influences selection thresholds: the presence or absence of certain types of items on the news menu raises or lowers the threshold for adding more of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a bulletin already has many foreign pieces of a certain type, the threshold for yet another foreign item of that type is increased; conversely, a lone domestic item may lower the threshold for adding a different kind of foreign item, in order to produce a balanced whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite nations (F9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events concerning 'elite' nations (big powers, highly consequential states) are more probable to become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: actions of elite nations tend to have greater short-term consequences; news is elite-centered geographically. Tabled as one of the culture-bound factors especially salient in northwestern media systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite people (F10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events concerning elite persons (leaders, celebrities, high officials) are more likely to be reported as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: elite actors are consequential and also serve as objects for general identification; stories about the elite can be used to tell about everybody. This is part of the observed elite-centeredness of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification / Personalization (F11)
rubrics_metrics.description: News tends to present events in personal terms (subject is a named person or small group) rather than as outcomes of impersonal social structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five offered explanations: (1) cultural idealism (focus on individual agency), (2) need for meaning/identification (persons facilitate projection and empathy), (3) frequency-fit (persons' actions fit media time-spans), (4) consequence of elite concentration, and (5) compatibility with modern news-gathering/presentation techniques (easier to photograph/interview a person than a structure). Personification reduces structural analysis and emphasizes human actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativization / Negativity (F12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative events (conflict, disaster, scandals) are more probable to be selected as news than positive events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple reasons offered: (1) negative events often satisfy frequency/time-span criteria more easily (they are quicker to occur), (2) negative events are more likely to be consensual/unambiguous, (3) negative news may fit dominant pre-images or high-anxiety matrices (cognitive dissonance), and (4) negative events are often more unexpected/rare. Predictions: during crises, unrelated news items become more negative; cultures that treat 'progress' as normal would over-report negative anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity hypothesis (newsworthiness scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event scores higher across the listed factors (the 12 factors), the higher its probability of becoming news and making headlines; events can be given a score from 0–12 representing newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: particular pairings (e.g., elite people in elite nations; negative events related to elite nations; scandals) are especially newsworthy. An event need not score 12 to be news — a threshold (floor) can be set (e.g., score ≥ 6) and many combinations can reach it. The paper uses additivity as a testable hypothesis about journalist/editor/reader behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Low score on one factor can be compensated by high score(s) on others; events may become news by different combinations of high-scoring factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally: for factors Fi and Fj, Fi low implies probability that some Fj is high is greater — complementarity generates many equivalent pathways to 'news'. Example: an event low on personal reference may need to be more negative to make the news (earthquakes presented as technical errors vs human factor). The hypothesis produces 66 pairwise testable implications for twelve factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication / Distortion across the news chain
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection and distortion operate at all steps in the chain from event to reader: each intermediary (correspondent, press agency, editor, layout) applies the same selection/distortion principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: longer chains produce more selection/distortion (but also more material to select from). The cumulative effects across links can produce an image of the world different from 'what really happened'. Research implication: observe how each link reacts to received material and replicates selection rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational/market and political orientation influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper characteristics (mass-circulation orientation, market incentives, tabloid vs broadsheet format, political line) shape selection and distortion — e.g., mass-circulation papers anticipate readers' reactions and accentuate selection to match perceived wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance: compare different newspapers (political leaning, morning vs afternoon, tabloid vs serious) to test replication and robustness; the authors selected newspapers across dimensions (radical/conservative, morning/afternoon) to provide replication. Organizational aims can increase or decrease emphasis on certain factors (e.g., ideological selection).
